headline.main: Chancellor Kickl?: The Right-Wing FPÖ Reaches for Power in Austria
headline.social: Chancellor Kickl?: The Right-Wing FPÖ Reaches for Power in Austria

intro: Herbert Kickl, who now has good chances of becoming Austria's next chancellor, has radicalized the FPÖ in recent years. He seems to enjoy his role as the ultimate evil.
text:
A middle-aged man in a dark suit walks into the hotel bar of the five-star Park Hyatt in Vienna and orders a fruit tea. Some of the guests recognize him, greeting him discreetly: "My compliments, Mr. Vice-Chancellor.”
Heinz-Christian Strache smiles and returns the greeting. The position of vice-chancellor is one he held until 2019 – in addition to having been the head of the right-wing populist Freedom Party of Austria (FPÖ) for 14 years. Then came the infamous Ibiza video, published by DER SPIEGEL and others – footage of Strache falling into a trap on the vacation island, blabbering without stop, and clearly demonstrating that he could be bought. It was the end of his political career.
Now, here he is in this half-empty hotel bar speaking about the comeback of the party that was once his life. About the recent successes of the FPÖ, which threw him out in 2019.
Two hours earlier on this Tuesday, Herbert Kickl, current leader of the FPÖ, had outlined the path he imagines will take him to the Austrian Chancellery. How he, exactly 100 days after the parliamentary elections at the end of September, intends to lead the FPÖ, a party with right-wing extremist elements, into power.
Mainly founded as a political home for former Nazis, the party, once called the VdU, has radicalized under Kickl’s leadership – and become significantly more popular. In the European right-wing context, the FPÖ is essentially an Austrian version of Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz in Hungary, Matteo Salvini’s Lega and the French right-wing party Rassemblement National. The FPÖ has primarily focused its attentions on the fight against illegal migration and is broadly pro-Moscow.
If Herbert Kickl is sworn in, he would already be the third Austrian chancellor this year, following Karl Nehammer, who resigned on Friday, and Alexander Schallenberg, who has been acting prime minister since then – a role he also briefly played in October 2021. Once again, the revolving doors are spinning in political Vienna. And once again, the FPÖ is at the center of the chaos.
Strache, who took over control of the FPÖ in 2005 at a time when the party was polling at a mere 3 percent, takes a sip of tea and says: "The Ibiza Affair distracts from the fact that we were the ones who established a 26-percent foundation back then, from which they are still benefiting. I think Kickl will be able to establish the FPÖ as a sustainable big-tent party and push the ÖVP” – the center-right Austrian People’s Party – permanently under the 20-percent mark. An historical window has opened up.”
The power-hungry, Christian-conservative ÖVP, "the black widow that eats up its coalition partners,” as the FPÖ camp has long charged: This Austrian big-tent party has been in freefall since the undoing of Sebastian Kurz in 2021 and, with the resignation announcement of party leader Chancellor Karl Nehammer, has become a caricature of itself. Acting party leader Christian Stocker has now been charged with doing that which had been strictly taboo until last Friday: form a coalition with the election victors from the FPÖ.
A Bathroom Break for the Goalkeeper
Kickl is a "well-oiled campaign and strategy machine,” says Strache approvingly, a politician with an unerring sense for what issues are on the top of voters’ minds. It was Strache himself, he claims, who took Kickl, that brash orator from Carinthia, under his wing more than two decades ago. He now believes Kickl has the stuff it takes to lead the Austrian government. "The other parties have gifted him the penalty shot. All he has to do is kick it into the goal.”
Political scientist Peter Filzmaier also uses the football analogy to describe the FPÖ’s current position, adding mockingly: "And the goalkeeper is currently taking a bathroom break.” The opponent, in other words, has abandoned the field without a fight.
The reference is to Austria’s mainstream parties: the ÖVP, the Social Democratic Party (SPÖ) and the economically liberal NEOS. After months of unsuccessful negotiations, the three parties announced on January 3 that there was insufficient common ground for building a coalition. Similar to Germany’s recently collapsed government, the trio of parties was unable to agree on how to shrink the county’s multi-billion-euro budgetary gap. Since then, finger pointing has become the new favorite pastime in political Vienna.
SPÖ party leader Andreas Babler, railed ÖVP leader Nehammer, had thwarted compromise with "class warfare rhetoric” and "retro” ideas. NEOS chairwoman Beate Meinl-Reisinger accused the SPÖ head of lying and choleric outbursts. Babler himself, the former mayor of the town of Traiskirchen and a self-defined Marxist, unsurprisingly has a different story to tell. The dejected SPÖ leader spoke in retrospect of "a brutal blame game that is completely unfounded.”
The FPÖ, which emerged from September elections as the strongest party in the country, was in the comfortable position of being able to lean back and watch the undignified spectacle unfold – "plenty of legroom in the first row,” as they say in Austria. All parties represented in Austrian parliament had categorically rejected the possibility of forming a coalition with the FPÖ under Kickl’s leadership. Until Christian Stocker then spoke on Sunday just over a week ago and heralded a complete reversal.
Stocker, a burly lawyer from the city of Wiener Neustadt, had only just been appointed ÖVP chairman when he rolled out the red carpet for the FPÖ. If the FPÖ sends an invitation to engage in coalition talks, Stocker said, "then we would accept it.” He justified his party’s change of tune by solemnly invoking his national political responsibility. It is not, he said, "about Herbert Kickl or myself.”
Be that as it may, the full scope of the current drama cannot be fully grasped without an examination of the actors in the leading roles. Just recently, Herbert Kickl was still referring to ÖVP leaders as "black political maggots,” as witless "imbeciles” and as "single-brain cell intellectuals.” The same politicians, in other words, who are now supposed to usher him into the Chancellery – and who apparently are interested in doing so as well.
"Kickl Stands for Political Extremism”
In the past, Kickl has always parried criticism of his choice of words by saying: "I’m not crude, I’m resolute.” There is, however, plenty of room for doubt about this self-serving estimation.
Kickl, after all, is now in the position of requiring the support of the ÖVP to build a stable government. In particular, he needs Christian Stocker’s backing.
Until the beginning of last week, the new head of the ÖVP was still dutifully channeling the chancellor, saying things like: "Herbert Kickl stands for political extremism.” As recently as December, he addressed the FPÖ leader directly, saying: "Nobody in this country needs you.”
Stocker warned that those who make political deals with Kickl will end up with "five dangerous years filled with radical ideas.” He then tried his hand at negotiating a coalition with SPÖ and NEOS. But the tripartite coalition failed, mocked by Kickl as a "political miscarriage” and "coalition of losers.”
And now these two firebrands from the FPÖ and ÖVP are supposed to join hands for the good of the republic? It is a constellation that seems too absurd to be true. But in Austria, things are sometimes possible that aren’t even under consideration elsewhere.
The FPÖ made clear a week ago on Tuesday just how the party imagines sharing power in a future coalition. Casually dressed in a suitcoat and open-collared shirt, Kickl shared his view of things, starting by painting a bleak picture of the current situation in Austria, most recently governed by the ÖVP together with the Greens. He spoke of the "money and trust” that had been gambled away,” of political "deadly sins” and of the "downfall” experienced in recent years. Kickl then tightened the rope around the throat of his future coalition partner: It is important not to forget, he said, who won the election – the FPÖ – "and who is not the victor” (the ÖVP). Some, he intimated, have apparently not yet completely understood this reality.
In other words: He, Kickl, is the man in charge. He wants to "pull his homeland out of the deep valley” and put it back on track to success. To ring in a new era – "with healthy patriotism and a pronounced love of freedom.” However, if his future coalition partner isn’t willing to govern "honestly,” then he will have to draw the consequences. "No games, no tricks, no sabotage.” Otherwise, says Kickl, "there will be new elections.”
The Return of Kurz?
According to the most recent polls, the FPÖ enjoys between 35 and 37 percent support. That equates to an additional 8 percentage points over the vote in September. Both the ÖVP and the SPÖ are wallowing in the neighborhood of 20 percent. The FPÖ, in other words, has less to fear from new elections than most of the other parties.
However, new elections could not take place before a majority vote in parliament. Should it come to that, there are some within the ÖVP who envision a return of the only serious rival to Kickl: Sebastian Kurz, the former Austrian chancellor. The one-time conservative wunderkind is, to be sure, still the focus of investigations into suspicions of embezzlement and bribery and has already been convicted in the first instance of giving false testimony. His unbroken political ambition, however, remains intact, say those in the know.
Thus far, new elections are only under consideration as a possible plan B. For now, the would-be coalition partners are feeling each other out, a process that began last Wednesday. That means that the beer-tent and social media rabble-rouser Kickl must increasingly focus his attentions on the nuts and bolts of government.
Talks with the ÖVP would face significant hurdles. For one, there isn’t much money for oiling compromises. On the contrary, the European Commission has threatened Austria with a deficit procedure due to the country’s elevated budgetary shortfalls. Vienna must cut spending by between 15 and 21 billion euros over the next four years.
A rendezvous with reality will likely make it clear to Kickl that he will find it challenging to fulfill even a fraction of his campaign promises. The FPÖ platform, called "Fortress Austria, Fortress of Freedom,” speaks of wide-ranging tax cuts and increased tax breaks for commuters. Paycheck withholdings are to be reduced significantly. One possibility for cutting spending would be the country’s multi-billion-euro involvement in the European air defense system Sky Shield. But it is doubtful whether the ÖVP would be willing to sacrifice this prestigious project.
Shameful Display
But the greatest challenges facing the battle-hardened pugilists from the FPÖ and ÖVP are in foreign and European policy. Kickl has never made secret his admiration for the autocratic governing style of Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. Particularly the manner in which Orbán has managed to rein in his country’s media and judiciary. In addition, Kickl was an early opponent of sanctions against Russia. When Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy appeared on the screen in Austrian parliament in March 2023 to begin his video address, Kickl and the rest of the FPÖ lawmakers walked out of the plenary hall.
It was a shameful yet telling display. The FPÖ continues to this day to oppose sanctions against the Russian invaders of Ukraine. On this point and others, the FPÖ will find itself in direct conflict with an ÖVP that has thus far been overtly pro-Ukraine and pro-Europe. The FPÖ campaigned with posters reading "Stop the EU Madness.” Should Kickl become chancellor, he could change Austria’s approach to Brussels.
In the "Patriotic Manifesto,” which Kickl presented in June together with Orbán of Hungary and the former Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš, the FPÖ leader fundamentally called into question EU migration policy in addition to the currency union and the bloc’s joint security policy. The FPÖ is also part of the Patriots for Europe group in European Parliament, where it rails against the EU in its current form in chorus with lawmakers from 12 other countries. Harald Vilimsky, the incumbent FPÖ floor leader in Brussels, is one of those party members who joined Strache on a 2016 trip to Moscow to hammer out a strategic cooperation deal with the Putin party United Russia, a journey commemorated with a few proud selfies on Red Square.
Herbert Kickl was not along for that particular ride. Even before that, he displayed a penchant for remaining on the sidelines, such as when one-time FPÖ demigod Jörg Haider and his acolytes were enjoying yet another bash. Or when Heinz Christian Strache joined fellow travelers from the Austrian fraternity scene for boozy evenings. Kickl, write is biographers Robert Treichler and Gernot Bauer, is the "most difficult chancellor candidate to assess” since the end of World War II. He is "a socially dysfunctional people’s tribune.”
A fundamentally shy person, Kickl only started enjoying interactions with the public a few years ago. Prior to that, he was happy to remain in the background, as an industrious worker in the party’s engine room. But in 2017, having been named interior minister by Chancellor Kurz against his will, the former philosophy student and hobby Hegelian suddenly found that the spotlight wasn’t so bad after all. An iconic image from 2018 shows the beaming interior minister proudly astride a horse.
"And he hasn’t dismounted since, if you will. He developed a taste for it,” says a former cabinet colleague. The ambitious FPÖ politician was thus unhappy to become the first and only minister to be relieved of his duties by an Austrian president since 1945 in the aftermath of the Ibiza Affair, for which he bore no responsibility.
Starting in 2020, Kickl established himself during the coronavirus pandemic at the head of a vociferous movement of anti-vaxxers and critics of measures implemented to slow the spread of the virus. His verbose complaints against alleged or actual state oppression raised his profile as a champion of freedom.
That experience found expression in the FPÖ’s campaign platform in the shape of a demand for a mechanism enabling the passage of laws independent of parliament. That mechanism foresees a mandatory, binding referendum if 250,000 signatures are gathered. Should a majority of voters be in favor, the proposal would become law. It is a procedure that would represent a fundamental rewriting of the rules thus far governing representative democracy.
"Repatriation of Uninvited Foreigners”
What drives someone like Kickl? The thought of being considered the ultimate evil, "of going down in history as Beelzebub, of which all are afraid,” doubtlessly exerts a pull on the FPÖ leader, says an adviser to the party. "He would love to be a disruptive factor, also on the European stage, like Orbán.”
Does that mean that a "People’s Chancellor” Kickl, as he has prematurely taken to calling himself, would introduce a new type of regime? Perhaps even the Orbánization of Austria, as Franz Fischler, a former European Commissioner from Austria, fears? Fischler has said he plans to leave the ÖVP should the party form a coalition with Kickl and the FPÖ.
Critics have warned that the media could be brought into line similar to the situation in Hungary, and that the judiciary could also face increased pressure. In the campaign platform, Kickl blathers about the "remigration of uninvited foreigners” – a phrase coined by right-wing extremists – and he also speaks of an alleged "population exchange.”
Which goals the FPÖ boss might actually be able to implement will largely depend on the drastically weakened ÖVP’s appetite for resistance. In addition, unlike Orbán in Budapest, Kickl would not enjoy a two-thirds parliamentary majority with an FPÖ-ÖVP coalition and would thus be unable to pass constitutional amendments.
Austrian President Alexander Van der Bellen has promised to demand respect for the "cornerstones of democracy.” It was Van der Bellen who dismissed Kickl from the Interior Ministry in 2019, and the president also seemed to indicate in 2023, as he was beginning his second term as head of state, that he wouldn’t be willing to swear in Kickl to the Chancellery. He said that as president, he would hardly be willing to empower "an anti-European party, a party that does not condemn Russia’s war against Ukraine.”
And now, two years and an FPÖ election victory later? Just over a week ago, Van der Bellen received Kickl through the red velvet doors of the former imperial chambers to discuss the future of the republic. The soon-to-be 81-year-old president showed no outward resentment for the fact that Kickl has referred to him in the past as the "mummy in the palace.” He was, however, open about the fact that he was not happy about the turn coalition talks had taken.
Unforgettable is the stony-faced expression of then-Austrian President Thomas Klestil when he received the architects of the first ÖVP-FPÖ coalition, later Chancellor Wolfgang Schüssel and FPÖ leader Jörg Haider, for talks a quarter century ago. Their alliance was accompanied by angry demonstrations and sanctions from the 14 EU member states back then. It ultimately ended with Haider’s withdrawal to his home state of Carinthia and the split of the FPÖ.
The second coalition between the two parties likewise did not end well. The crisis of state triggered by the Ibiza video ended with the FPÖ’s withdrawal from the coalition and the collapse of Chancellor Sebastian Kurz’s first government. The investigations launched by public prosecutors at the time into suspicions of corruption, abuse of office and embezzlement in parts of the government continue to occupy the Austrian judiciary to this day.
Will the FPÖ, under its disciplinarian leader Herbert Kickl, be able to shed its reputation as a party that reliably self-implodes as soon as it becomes part of government? The ascetic Kickl, an extreme triathlete in his spare time, is seen as far less likely than his predecessors to fall victim to a lack of self-control. On the contrary: The concern is more that of a systemic crisis stemming from an increasing urge to exert control.
It was Kickl who, as interior minister in 2018, was partly responsible for an armed raid on BVT, the country’s domestic intelligence agency at the time, for alleged corruption. The commando operation was a disaster. Kickl was suspected of having targeted undesirable agents for political reasons and the police confiscated confidential documents. The international reputation of Austrian secret service agencies was damaged and remains so today. Later came suspicions that the BVT may have been infiltrated by Russian spies.
Kickl has said that his preferred activity for recuperating from the rigors of his job is mountain climbing. During the last campaign, he was asked when he thought he would finally be able to relax a bit. The response of the FPÖ leader: "Maybe once we have achieved our great goal.”
He meant: Moving into the Chancellery on Ballhausplatz in Vienna.
